clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder combining progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, and cancer predisposition
Progressive ataxia usually appears in early childhood as a child begins to walk, followed by dysarthria and abnormal eye movements (oculomotor apraxia)
Telangiectasias typically develop later, most visibly on the bulbar conjunctivae and sun-exposed skin
Combined humoral and cellular immunodeficiency leads to recurrent sinopulmonary infections
Markedly elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein is a characteristic and useful laboratory clue
Caused by biallelic mutations in the ATM gene, whose product is central to detecting and repairing DNA double-strand breaks
Extreme radiosensitivity means diagnostic and therapeutic ionising radiation must be minimised
Substantially increased risk of malignancy, particularly lymphoid cancers, and carriers may have modestly raised cancer risk
reference.pathophysiology: Ataxia-telangiectasia is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the ATM gene, which encodes a kinase that senses DNA double-strand breaks and coordinates the cellular response, including cell-cycle arrest, DNA repair, and apoptosis. Loss of ATM function leaves cells unable to respond properly to DNA damage, causing genomic instability, heightened sensitivity to ionising radiation, and a strong predisposition to malignancy. Progressive death of cerebellar Purkinje and granule cells produces the characteristic neurodegeneration and ataxia, while impaired lymphocyte development and class-switching cause the combined immunodeficiency. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Friedreich ataxia and other hereditary ataxias
Ataxia with oculomotor apraxia types 1 and 2
Nijmegen breakage syndrome and related DNA-repair disorders
additionalInvestigations: ATM molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Immunological evaluation of immunoglobulin levels and lymphocyte subsets
Radiosensitivity or chromosomal instability studies where available
Neuroimaging showing cerebellar atrophy and developmental assessment
redFlags: Extreme radiosensitivity making conventional-dose ionising radiation potentially harmful, so imaging and cancer therapy require specialist modification
High risk of lymphoma and leukaemia requiring vigilance for suggestive symptoms
Progressive respiratory decline from recurrent infection and aspiration
Immunodeficiency raising the risk of severe infection
reference.prognosis: The condition is progressive, with most affected individuals becoming wheelchair-dependent by adolescence and life expectancy reduced, chiefly due to malignancy and chronic respiratory disease.
pitfalls: Exposing patients to standard-dose radiation before recognising the diagnosis
Attributing early ataxia to cerebral palsy and missing the syndrome
Overlooking the diagnostic value of a raised alpha-fetoprotein
Underestimating the lifelong cancer surveillance and infection-prevention needs
management: Supportive neurorehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and swallowing therapy and mobility aids for the progressive ataxia

Management of the combined immunodeficiency with immunoglobulin replacement where indicated, prompt treatment of sinopulmonary infections, appropriate vaccination and prophylaxis, and airway-clearance and respiratory care
Minimisation of diagnostic and therapeutic ionising radiation and of radiomimetic chemotherapy because of marked cellular radiosensitivity
Active malignancy surveillance for lymphoma and leukaemia, with prompt investigation of unexplained symptoms
Nutritional support and aspiration precautions as bulbar function declines
Multidisciplinary follow-up across neurology, immunology and respiratory medicine
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder, with family and carrier testing
